passages.retrieved_command: curl -sS -L --max-time 150 -A "Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64)" -o krahmalkov.txt "https://dn721606.ca.archive.org/0/items/phoenician-punic-dictionary-charles-r.-krahmalkov/Phoenician-Punic%20Dictionary%20-%20Charles%20R.%20Krahmalkov_djvu.txt"  -> HTTP 200, 898880 bytes, sha256 77c9ba632da9d4328a410115d945972b32ccb1955dead1ca90ac689a624def28
passages.source_locator: entry MLQRT (B'L SR), printed p. 290 (= text-layer lines 16216-16231 of the retrieved djvu.txt); components at entries MLK III (lines 15869-15879), MLK IV (lines 15881-15888) and QRT I (lines 24488-24499)
passages.source_excerpt: "MLQRT (B'L SR) — d. MILQART, principal deity of the city of Tyre; the full name was MILQART, THE BAAL (PROPRIETARY GOD) OF TYRE. KAI 47.1 (Ph) l'dnn Imlqrt b'l sr, <Dedicated> to our lord, Milqart, the proprietary god of Tyre. Passim. Frequent in Ph and Pu personal names, in which the name is sometimes found in the abbreviated form qrt, Qart: see QRT II." | component MLK III: "[Heb. melek] n.m. KING — KAI 1.1 (Ph) 'hrm mlk gbl, 'Ahiram, King of Byblos.'" | component QRT I, pl. QORHT: "[Heb. geret, girya] n.f. CITY — KAI 26 A II 9/10 (Ph) wbn 'nk hqrt z … 'And I built this city …'; … KAI 26 A III 5 (Ph) kl 'ln grt, 'All the gods of the city.'" | MLK IV: "d. MILK ('The King'), the byname of the god Il, king of the gods"
passages.ocr_caveat: Quoted from the archive.org djvu text layer, not from the printed page: the OCR renders MLQRT as 'MLORT' in headings, BAAL as 'BASAL' in the MLQRT entry, and qeret as 'geret' in the QRT I bracket. Word boundaries and diacritics are OCR-approximate; wording and structure follow the scan.
passages.passage_support: Establishes, from a standard epigraphic lexicon reached by a channel neither round 8 nor a museum-record hunter uses: (i) the name's two components are lexically 'king' (mlk) and 'city' (qrt) in Phoenician/Punic, with published epigraphic citations on each; (ii) the god's standing proprietary title in the inscriptions is b'l sr, 'Baal (proprietary god) of Tyre' (KAI 47.1 quoted verbatim), which is the civic formula the entry's claim treats as the productive semantic; (iii) the divine name is abbreviated to qrt in personal names, giving a lexicographic anchor for the ʿbdmlqrt-type name row at entry line 146.
passages.calibration: Important negative nuance, stated plainly: Krahmalkov's entry does NOT print the composite gloss 'king of the city'. He glosses the god as 'Milqart' with the title 'Baal of Tyre'. The composite translation remains an interpretive gloss carried by the narrative literature (see passages 2-3), not a dictionary entry line.

passages.source_locator: section 'El templo fenicio y el Melqart de Tiro' (running head 'LAS GRANDES INSTITUCIONES POLÍTICAS 137' immediately precedes it; text-layer lines 7263-7286 and 7416-7498, between the running heads for printed pp. 140 and 142) and the continuation at text-layer lines 7552-7566 between the running heads for pp. 142 and 146
passages.source_excerpt: (a) "El dios era el señor de la ciudad y, como tal, ejercía su autoridad sobre la comunidad, organizada en torno a su templo." | (b) "En un principio, el Melqart de Tiro pudo ser una divinización del propio rey de la ciudad, el m/k-qrt. De ser así, Melgart, el dios nacional tirio, sería la exaltación teológica del rey y, como tal, el antepasado de la ciudad, la hipóstasis del rey y, en definitiva, el mismo rey." | (c) "Como dios del mar, era el patrón de la navegación y del comercio." | (d) "Con motivo de la fundación de una colonia o enclave comercial, la costumbre tiria exigía construir un templo en honor de Melqart. Ello creaba un vínculo religioso entre la colonia y la metrópoli, y la presencia del dios en tierras lejanas aseguraba la tutela del templo de Tiro en esa empresa. En otras palabras, la presencia de Melqart garantizaba o advertía de la intervención de la monarquía en toda actividad comercial lejana." | (e) "la función de los santuarios de Melqart en Occidente consistió en servir de nexo de unión entre Tiro y los centros comerciales mediterráneos. A cambio de velar por la buena marcha de la navegación y del comercio, Melgart recibía la décima parte de las ganancias obtenidas. Su función no fue, así, exclusivamente religiosa, sino básicamente política: asegurar la dependencia de Cádiz o de Cartago con relación a Tiro."
passages.ocr_caveat: OCR layer; the ligature is rendered 'm/k-qrt' where the print plausibly reads 'mlk-qrt' (quoted as printed by the OCR, not silently corrected); 'Melqart'/'Melgart' spellings alternate exactly as the OCR gives them.
passages.passage_support: This is the decisive alternate-angle find for the anti-fixing leg and for the attribution chain. (1) The book that Wikipedia's trader-protector sentence relays states the composite analysis itself, in the king-of-the-city direction: 'pudo ser una divinización del propio rey de la ciudad, el [m]lk-qrt' — i.e. the entry's line-78 gloss is exactly what the relay's own source says. (2) The same source frames the commercial function as royal political integration: the god's presence 'garantizaba o advertía de la intervención de la monarquía en toda actividad comercial lejana'; the Western sanctuaries worked as links between Tyre and Mediterranean commercial centres, and their function was 'no … exclusivamente religiosa, sino básicamente política'. (3) Crucially, the source DOES attribute navigation-and-commerce patronage to the god ('era el patrón de la navegación y del comercio'), as one function inside a city-and-kingship profile — so a commercial role is not absent from the literature; what the entry denies (a single fixed 'patron of merchants' job) is not what the sources describe, and the entry must not be tightened into a denial of commercial functions (this is round-8 limit 6, now demonstrated against the relay's own source rather than against the tertiary page).
passages.note: Page bracket, measured not asserted: the quotes in (a)-(d) sit in the text layer between the running heads '140 TIRO Y LAS COLONIAS FENICIAS DE OCCIDENTE' and '142 TIRO Y LAS COLONIAS FENICIAS DE OCCIDENTE', i.e. printed pp. 140–141 (quote (a) follows the head for p. 137); quote (e) sits between the heads for pp. 142 and 146.

passages.source_excerpt: p. 446 (retrieved page text): "Personnification de la planète Saturne (W. Genesius) ou dieu du feu (F. K. Movers) ; divinité solaire (W. W. Baudissin) ou infernale (W. F. (i) The composite gloss 'roi de la cité (mlk qrt)' is stated inside a peer review of the entry's named authority, and the same extract quotes the book itself ('… à l'altération du personnage divin appelé Melqart » (P- 9)') — so Bonnet 1988's argument is now reached through peer assessment even though the book's body text is unread. (ii) The retrieved p. 446 text is the strongest single passage yet for the 'limits of a fixed profile' half of the question: a peer review enumerates at least ten mutually incompatible modern definitions of Melqart (Saturn personification, fire god, solar, infernal, storm-and-rain, agrarian, Baal-Hadad+Yam syncretism, sea god, El himself, god of conquest), i.e. the literature itself fails to fix one theological profile — exactly what the entry's line 78 refuses to do.

passages.source_excerpt: "Milqart, le grand dieu de Tyr et le protecteur de l'expansion commerciale de la cité, n'avait jusqu'ici, curieusement, fait l'objet que d'articles partiels et souvent vieillis. La synthèse magistrale que nous propose C. Bonnet est donc particulièrement bienvenue."
passages.passage_support: A second, independent peer assessment of the unread book. Its framing matters for calibration in the direction round-8 limit 6 flagged: a specialist reviewer describes Melqart as 'le grand dieu de Tyr et le protecteur de l'expansion commerciale de la cité' — i.e. a commercial-expansion role is part of how the god is summarised by reviewers of Bonnet's own book, alongside the civic title. passages.source_citation: Comte du Mesnil du Buisson, 'Origine et évolution du panthéon de Tyr', Revue de l'histoire des religions 164-2 (1963), pp. 133-163

Extract retrieved via: curl -sS --http1.1 --max-time 60 -A "Mozilla/5.0" -o persee_search.html "https://www.persee.fr/search?ta=article&q=Melqart+%22roi+de+la+cit%C3%A9%22" -> HTTP 200, 304691 bytes

passages.source_excerpt: "… al de Tyr, le « maître de la ville », ou comme son surnom l'indique, le « roi de la cité ». … On a proposé de comprendre le nom de Melqart : « le Roi de la Cité infernale », parce que le monde souterrain est appelé « la Cité » dans un texte…"
passages.passage_support: Tests the entry's hedge word 'understood as'. The literature contains (i) the entry's gloss ('roi de la cité'), (ii) a variant title ('maître de la ville'), and (iii) a rival analysis where the second element refers to the netherworld ('le Roi de la Cité infernale' — i.e. qrt read as the underworld 'City'). The entry's choice of the conventional gloss with 'is understood as' rather than 'means' is therefore calibrated; a future revision may not drop the hedge.
passages.media_caveat: Displayed-extract retrieval only, for the gloss sentences; the article's own pages were not read.

basis: Alternate-angle escalation produced passage-level support on channels round 8 did not use, and closed the repertory question with a host-level diagnosis. (1) The name analysis: Aubet's monograph — the very source relayed by the designated tertiary page — states the composite directly in the king-of-the-city direction ('una divinización del propio rey de la ciudad, el [m]lk-qrt', pp. 140-141), the RÉA 1990 review extract of Bonnet 1988 states 'le « roi de la cité » (mlk qrt)', and Krahmalkov's dictionary gives the components in their published epigraphic uses (mlk = KING, qrt = CITY) while glossing the god by his standing civic title 'Baal (proprietary god) of Tyre' (KAI 47.1). (2) The anti-fixing leg: Aubet frames the Western sanctuaries as links in Tyre's royal commercial policy ('básicamente política', pp. 142-145), and the RÉA review's p. 446 text documents ten incompatible modern definitions of the god — i.e. the scholarly literature itself does not fix a single profile. (3) Calibration in both directions: the same source that supports the civic reading also attributes commerce-patronage to the god, and the Syria review sums him up as protector of the city's commercial expansion — so the entry's 'more productive than … alone' wording is right and must not be tightened. (4) The attribution '(Bonnet 1988)' itself is still not verified at book level, but it is no longer unapproached: two independent peer reviews of the book and a displayed extract quoting the book's p. 9 were retrieved, and Bonnet's 2009 author-direct deposit on Melqart in the diaspora is confirmed to exist on HAL (text blocked by a bot challenge). (5) The repertory is definitively closed by the host-level finding.

deeper_limit_receipt.what_would_close_them: A library or ILL copy of Bonnet 1988 (or its Carthage chapter), a browser-driven session for HAL/OpenEdition/Persée downloads, and a physical or digitized copy of Lipiński 2002. limits: 1) No passage in this receipt comes from the printed page of a book I could open page-by-page: Krahmalkov and Aubet were read through scan OCR text layers (OCR artifacts flagged per passage), and the RÉA/Syria/RHR gloss sentences came from Persée's displayed extracts, not from the review articles' own pages where the sentences are printed. Quotations are reproduced exactly as the retrieved text layers render them, including OCR spellings. 2) The composite gloss 'king of the city' is an interpretive statement about the divine name, not a dictionary headword: Krahmalkov glosses components and the title Baal of Tyre, not the compound. 3) The '(Bonnet 1988)' attribution stays unverified at book level; what is verified is that (a) two peer reviews of the book exist and were reached, (b) one displayed extract quotes the book's p. 9, and (c) the book's record on HAL has no deposited text. 4) The rival 'Cité infernale' reading is documentation that the gloss is contested in the literature, not an endorsement that it is correct; it also rests on a displayed extract rather than a page read. 5) Aubet's page numbers are running-head brackets from OCR, not verified folios. 6) The merchant-patron framing appearing on the designated tertiary page is a compression of Aubet's politically-framed statements; do not read my passages as proof that no commercial-patron reading of Melqart exists — Aubet says the opposite.
coupling_implication: Unchanged in direction from round 8, now grounded in the relay's own source and in the book's reviews: model a city god whose profile is assembled from the city's institutional life (proprietary god of the city, divine double of kingship, oath and treaty god, temple network as political-commercial infrastructure) rather than from a single occupational patronage; treat commercial patronage as one office the god can hold inside that institutional frame, not as his definition; and treat 'king of the city' as a conventional reading with at least one rival in the scholarship — keep the hedge. For the lane's handoff: the evidence base changes by city, century and channel (Aramaic stele of the 9th/8th c. BCE; 2nd-c. BCE Maltese bilingual; Roman-imperial coins of Tyre; Punic personal names), so a world bible should date each Melqart function to its witness rather than to a single reconstructed theology.
open_questions: 1) Book-level closure still requires Bonnet 1988 itself (pp. 165-201 for the Carthage argument); the next cheapest route found is a library/ILL copy, since every open channel is exhausted as of this round. 2) A browser-assisted (non-automated) download of HAL hal-01996916 would give Bonnet's own 2009 wording on Melqart as ancestral god of the diaspora — the single most valuable remaining author-direct statement. 3) If the lane wants the onomastic claim on entry line 146 (ʿbdmlqrt as ordinary morphology), Benz's Personal Names in the Phoenician and Punic Inscriptions is indexed in the Open Library search-inside corpus and is a direct target. 4) The 'Cité infernale' rival reading deserves a page-level check in RHR 164-2 (1963) if the claim's hedge is ever revisited.
